PASSO 1: pense em uma história como em u: STEP 1: think of a story like a movie. First comes the setting: the time, the weather, the place, how people were. Then come the events, one after another. STEP 2: the setting goes in the imperfecto, because it's ongoing with no marked start or end: «Eran las ocho, hacía frío y yo esperaba el autobús» (it was eight, it was cold, and I was waiting for the bus). STEP 3: each event goes in the indefinido, because it starts and ends: «De repente llegó Marta y me saludó» (suddenly Marta arrived and said hello). STEP 4: ask each verb two questions. «Did this happen once and finish?» Then use the indefinido. «Was this ongoing, or how things were at that moment?» Then use the imperfecto. STEP 5: when an ongoing action gets interrupted, the ongoing one goes in the imperfecto and the one that interrupts goes in the indefinido: «Dormía cuando sonó el teléfono» (I was sleeping when the phone rang). STEP 6: a sequence of events, one after another, all stays in the indefinido: «Llegué, abrí la puerta, vi una carta y la leí» (I arrived, opened the door, saw a letter, and read it). STEP 7: the markers help. Indefinido: ayer, un día, aquel día, de repente, el lunes, una vez, a las tres. Imperfecto: siempre, cada día, todos los veranos, de niño, mientras, normalmente. STEP 8: in Spain, for a period that hasn't ended (esta mañana, hoy), the event uses the pretérito perfecto, while the setting stays in the imperfecto: «Esta mañana llovía y he llevado el paraguas». In Latin America people say «Esta mañana llovía y llevé el paraguas».
o português faz a mesma separação, quase: English's simple past covers both roles here with no change in form at all — «it was raining» (ongoing) and «it rained» (a finished event) are the closest English gets, using «was/were + -ing» versus the plain past, but English speakers routinely blur that line in casual speech. Spanish forces the choice every single time, with two completely different verb forms, so this lesson's two questions — «did it happen once and finish?» versus «was it ongoing or how things were?» — aren't a check on something you already do instinctively; they're a habit to build from scratch.

PASSO 1: quatro verbos mudam de sentido: STEP 1: four verbs shift meaning depending on which past tense they're in. «Sabía» means «I already knew»; «supe» means «I found out (at that moment)». «Conocía a Ana» means «I already knew Ana»; «conocí a Ana» means «I met Ana for the first time». STEP 2: «quería salir» means «I wanted to leave», with no word on whether I actually did; «quise salir» means «I tried to leave», and «no quise salir» means «I refused to leave». STEP 3: «podía salir» means «I had the option of leaving»; «pude salir» means «I managed to leave», and «no pude salir» means «I wasn't able to leave». STEP 4: «había» is the imperfecto of «hay» and sets the scene: «Había mucha gente en la plaza» (there were a lot of people in the square). STEP 5: «hubo» is the indefinido of «hay» and reports a specific event: «Hubo un accidente en la plaza» (there was an accident in the square). Both are invariable: «había dos personas», «hubo dos accidentes» — never «habían» or «hubieron». STEP 6: judging a whole, finished event calls for the indefinido: «La fiesta fue genial» (the party was great). Describing how the party was at a given moment calls for the imperfecto: «La fiesta era genial, pero yo estaba cansado» (the party was great, but I was tired). STEP 7: a closed period, even a long one, calls for the indefinido: «Viví tres años en Lima» (I lived in Lima for three years); with no stated limit, the imperfecto: «Vivía en Lima» (I used to live in Lima). STEP 8: «salir de» means to leave a place («Salí del trabajo a las seis»); «irse» means to go away, to take off («Se fue a las seis»); «salir con alguien» means to go out with someone, in the sense of dating («Salió con Marta»).
o português tem os mesmos pares com sent: English has exactly this same split in meaning for «knew/found out» and «could/managed to», so the underlying logic isn't new — «I knew» versus «I found out», «I could leave» versus «I managed to leave» are real, distinct ideas in English too, just expressed with different words rather than a tense swap on the same verb. What's new is «había» versus «hubo»: English «there was» covers both the backdrop sense (there were a lot of people) and the single-event sense (there was an accident) with the exact same words, so nothing in English flags that Spanish treats these as two different grammatical choices.

PASSO 1: uma boa narração tem três parte: STEP 1: a good narration has three parts: the setting (imperfecto), the problem or event (indefinido), and the outcome (indefinido). STEP 2: useful connectors: «al principio» opens it, «entonces» and «de repente» move the story forward, «por eso» gives the consequence, and «al final» closes it. STEP 3: the setting can come back in the middle of the story when something needs explaining: «Tenía prisa, porque mi hermana cumplía años» (I was in a hurry, because it was my sister's birthday). STEP 4: the weather follows the same rule. «Llovía mucho» describes the setting; «Llovió toda la noche» sums up a closed period. STEP 5: in Latin America, «parada» and «cumplir años» are understood everywhere; for «bus», some regions say «colectivo», «guagua», or «camión», depending on the country.
os conectores do português têm equivalen: English's connectors map onto these almost one for one: «al principio» is «at first», «por eso» is «so» or «that's why», and «al final» is «in the end». Watch the difference between «al final» (in the end, as the story wraps up) and «por fin» (finally, after a wait): «Al final fuimos» (in the end we went) versus «¡Por fin llegó el autobús!» (the bus finally showed up!) — English «finally» can cover both senses, where Spanish keeps them as two separate phrases.
